newsitem.title: FRANCE: Versace was master of glamour but not innovation.
newsitem.headline: Versace was master of glamour but not innovation.

text.p: The gunman who killed Italian designer Gianni Versace on the steps of his Miami Beach mansion robbed the showbiz world of a master of Hollywood glamour and overt sexuality.
But history is unlikely to remember him as one of the great fashion designers of the century, unlike Yves Saint Laurent, Christian Dior or Giorgio Armani.
Versace, who once said that a woman who wore his clothes inevitably had a lover, unabashedly created a universe of luxury and glitz for golden girls with vast fortunes and personal trainers.
"I dress the nouveau riche. So what? Don't forget that's what the old rich once were," Versace told an interviewer in 1996.
He leaves a legacy of beautifully made modern clothes with clean lines that are sinuous and provocative.

Still, Versace was less known for the type of ground-breaking innovation that changes the direction of fashion than for his dangerously slinky and glamorous gowns paraded by supermodels who took a fortune for their services in catwalk extravaganzas.
Some critics sneered at him, criticising what they considered his lack of good taste.
Versace's list of customers read like a Who's Who of the international jet-set: Elton John, Madonna, Prince, Sting, Mick Jagger, Liz Hurley and Princess Diana.

"He opened this decade with the spectacle of his ultra-clingy minidresses, fluorescent, zipped, bejewelled, embroidered and hugging the bodies of man-eaters and other siliconed stars," wrote Laurence Benaim, fashion writer for the respected French daily Le Monde.

Versace's sensuous and often ostentatious collections -- sequined gowns with plunging necklines and daring slits -- were simultaneously flavoured with ancient Roman and Greek influences, and neo-Punk.

"Gianni knew how to bring out the best in a woman's body better than anyone else...flirting with the slutty side of Italian women with fantastic cheek and humour to the point of idealising them," said French designer Thierry Mugler, who regularly bumped into the couturier aboard the Concorde.
Versace's style was best immortalised in a much-copied gown designed for Liz Hurley -- a wisp of black crepe fastened down the side with giant safety pins.

"His creations were immediately recognisable: rich, glamorous and sexy. He was courageous enough to use a good dose of vulgarity in a splendid way," said Mary Quant, the British designer who invented the mini-skirt.
A man of humble origins, Versace was born in Reggio Calabria, in the poor south of Italy, and learned the fashion trade from his mother, a local dressmaker.

As his company, launched in 1972 with his brother Santo and sister Donatella, who was his muse and artistic director, grew to be a $875 million empire, Versace's lifestyle became akin to that of the women who bought his clothes: opulent and decadent.

He was known as a big spender, renting the swimming pool of Paris's Ritz Hotel for his fashion shows and lining the walls of his marbled bathroom in Miami with paintings by Picasso and Renoir. He had a third residence, an olympian villa on Lake Como.
Media reports citing close associates of the designer say that Donatella will probably take over the fashion side of things while Santo continues his role as business and financial manager.
